title: Conformance probes for JSON structured output
body:
Purpose:
This is a working prompt bank + runbook for running JSON conformance probes during model onboarding and regressions. Focus: structured-output fidelity and tolerant-but-predictable handling of real-world noisy inputs. Use these probes to surface formatter regressions (different quoting, trailing commas), type drift (numbers returned as strings), structural drift (missing/extra keys), and semantic regressions (wrong enum values).

Scope:
- Target models: production and candidate family checkpoints used in hosted/dedicated/private deploys.
- Test surface: JSON syntax, JSON Schema adherence (required types/enums), canonical field semantics (timestamps, ids), and robustness to input mutations.
- Intended for: applied-ml engineers running onboarding evals, SREs validating API contracts, and product owners verifying backward compatibility.

How to use this doc:
1) Pick the candidate model and load the latest prompt templates from this file.
2) Run the prompt set over a representative seed set (n >= 200) including heavy mutation variants below.
3) Validate with a strict JSON parser (syntax) + JSON Schema validator (semantics). We recommend ajv (node) or jsonschema (python).
4) Score and triage failures; file regression tickets with reproducible prompt+seed+model.

Scoring rubric (quick):
- Syntax check (0/1): 1 if parsable JSON returned, 0 otherwise.
- Schema check (0/2): 2 if validator passes exactly, 1 if passes with non-fatal type coercion (e.g., numeric strings convertible), 0 if required fields missing or type mismatch not coercible.
- Semantics check (0/2): 2 if field-level semantics match canonical expectations (valid timestamp format, id patterns, enums), 1 if minor deviations (timezone omission but parseable), 0 for wrong semantics (e.g., incorrect enum meaning).
Total per-example: 0-5. Aggregate metrics: percent of examples with score == 5, mean score, and top-5 failure modes.

Validator configuration suggestions:
- ajv --strict false, allErrors true for initial pass (report everything). For final gating, run ajv with strict mode and no coercion.
- python jsonschema.validate with format-checkers for date-time.

Prompt bank overview (templates + variants):
Note: prompts intentionally vary instruction style: direct schema injection, role prompts, and few-shot examples. Keep prompt templates short; include the JSON Schema inline when gating is strict.

1) Minimal schema prompt (direct):
PROMPT_MINIMAL_SCHEMA:
"You are a strict JSON generator. Output only JSON, no surrounding commentary. Produce a single object that matches this schema exactly. Schema: {\n  \"type\": \"object\",\n  \"required\": [\"user_id\", \"events\"],\n  \"properties\": {\n    \"user_id\": {\"type\": \"string\"},\n    \"events\": {\"type\": \"array\", \"items\": {\"type\": \"object\", \"required\": [\"ts\", \"name\"], \"properties\": {\"ts\": {\"type\": \"string\", \"format\": \"date-time\"}, \"name\": {\"type\": \"string\"}, \"props\": {\"type\": \"object\"}}}}\n  }\n}\nGenerate an example with 2 events."

Expected canonical output (example):
{"user_id":"u_12345","events":[{"ts":"2025-10-01T12:34:56Z","name":"login","props":{}},{"ts":"2025-10-02T08:20:00Z","name":"purchase","props":{"amount":12.5}}]}

Stress variants for this prompt (mutations to feed model or to instruct model to be permissive):
- Ask for trailing comma in example (model should NOT include trailing commas).
- Switch quotes to single quotes.
- Request top-level array instead of object.
- Request keys in different order.
- Embed comments (// or /* */) in the JSON.
- Put numeric values as strings (\"12.5\").
- Return ISO date without timezone (2025-10-01T12:34:56) or epoch milliseconds.
- Include unexpected extra keys in event objects.
- Duplicate keys with different values.

2) Role-based few-shot (soft constraints):
PROMPT_ROLE_FEWSHOT:
"You are a data formatter for the analytics team. Below are three examples of the event envelope we expect. When writing your output, return only JSON and follow examples. Example 1: {\"user_id\":\"u_x\",\"events\":[{\"ts\":\"2024-01-01T00:00:00Z\",\"name\":\"signup\",\"props\":{}}]}\nExample 2: {\"user_id\":\"u_y\",\"events\":[{\"ts\":\"2024-02-01T12:00:00Z\",\"name\":\"view\",\"props\":{\"page\":\"home\"}}]}\nInstruction: produce one object like those with two events."

This style often increases correct shape but can still produce subtle syntax errors under model regressions.

3) Error-injection prompt (adversarial):
PROMPT_ADVERSARIAL_SHORT:
"Return JSON only. Intentionally include a trailing comma and a comment in the second event. Then also add an extra key 'debug' set to null."

Use this prompt to verify the parser/validator rejects known-bad outputs and to check whether the model obeys adversarial instructions (we often see models follow the adversarial instruction instead of correcting).

Targeted test cases (high priority):
- Missing required field 'user_id'.
- events is string instead of array.
- event.ts as unix epoch integer instead of RFC3339 string.
- props contains HTML or markdown that should be allowed as string but not as nested JSON.
- enum-like field 'name' uses capitalized variants or synonyms (\"Purchase\" vs \"purchase\").
- Numeric overflow: very large integers returned as strings or scientific notation.
- Duplicate keys: parser behavior depends on library; flag duplicates as failure for strict gating.

Mutation battery (generate variations programmatically):
For each base prompt, produce N mutated prompts by applying the following transforms to the seed examples or prompt instruction. The mutations are intentionally realistic, reflecting user-provided prompt noise.
- Quoting changes: double -> single, escape sequences introduced.
- Whitespace and line breaks: compact one-line vs pretty-printed.
- Type coercion: numbers as strings, booleans as strings, nulls inserted.
- Structural flips: swap array <-> object for small subtrees.
- Encoding: add BOM, non-ASCII characters in keys/values (emojis, accented chars).
- Partial output: truncated JSON (simulate early termination).
- Extra wrapping: model returns a string containing JSON (i.e., escaped JSON string).
- Markdown wrapper: output enclosed in ```json ``` fences.

Examples of mutation outcomes we expect to catch:
- \"events\": \"[{...}]\"
- Trailing comma: {\"a\":1,}
- Comments present: /* debug */{\"a\":1}
- Escaped JSON string: \"{\\\"user_id\\\":\\\"u\\\"}\"

Regression triage checklist (when failure rate increases):
- Capture failing prompt + seed + model checkpoint + raw response.
- Run syntactic parse; if parse fails, log parser error and attach to ticket.
- If parse succeeds but schema fails, attach validator errors (which properties failed).
- Compare with last passing checkpoint: diff by token-level alignment to see where structure deviated (use ed-level diff tools).
- Quick experiments: 1) re-run with minimal system prompt that says "Output only JSON" 2) add a tiny few-shot canonical example 3) lower temperature / set deterministic decoding.

Automated checks to include in CI harness:
- Syntax pass rate >= 98% for gate; otherwise block.
- Schema pass rate >= 95% (configurable per product).
- Semantic pass (timestamp format + id regex) >= 98%.
- Monitor shifting failure modes; create alerts for sudden increase in trailing-comma or comment patterns.

Example checklist for a single eval run:
- [ ] Seed set selected (id of dataset).
- [ ] Prompt templates loaded (list and versions).
- [ ] Model checkpoint noted.
- [ ] Parser and validator versions recorded.
- [ ] Run completed and artifacts stored (raw responses + parsed JSON).
- [ ] Aggregate scores computed and uploaded to dashboard.

Notes to reviewers / open questions:
- Should we allow numeric-as-string for legacy pipelines? (short term: allow with warning, long term: block for critical fields)
- How to handle duplicates: some JSON libraries keep last value, others first; we should treat duplicates as failure for strict gates.
- Do we want an "auto-fix" layer that attempts canonicalization (coerce types, convert timestamps) and then re-validate? If yes, need to codify safe transforms.

Appendix: Short list of concrete prompts to run (copy/paste friendly)
1) Strict schema injection (see PROMPT_MINIMAL_SCHEMA above)
2) Role-based few-shot (see PROMPT_ROLE_FEWSHOT)
3) Adversarial injection (PROMPT_ADVERSARIAL_SHORT)
4) Wrapper-check prompt:
"Return only the JSON object, NOT wrapped in markdown or text. If you must show code fences remove them. Expected schema: <paste schema>."
5) Escape-test prompt:
"Produce a JSON object as a single string value (i.e., return an escaped JSON string). Then produce the same object as an object. We want both variants to test detection of escaped wrappers."

Quick run example (local):
- node run_eval.js --model candidate-v2 --prompts conformance-probes-for-json-output.json --out results/candidate-v2.jsonl
- python validate_results.py --schema schemas/event-envelope.json --results results/candidate-v2.jsonl --report reports/candidate-v2-summary.json

TODOs:
- [ ] Add more seeded examples with multi-locale timestamps (PT/UTC/CET). Owner: Ethan. ETA: 2026-03-20.
- [ ] Bake this prompt set into onboarding pipeline and add dashboarding for top failure classes. Owner: Priya.
- [ ] Document safe coercion transforms and publish to ops repo. Owner: Maya.

Short retrospective note: during last onboarding run (candidate-v1 -> promoted), we observed a spike in outputs wrapped in triple backticks; adding explicit instruction to remove fences and adding 3 deterministic examples reduced that failure class by ~85%. Keep that pattern in new tests.

Contact: Maya Patel (applied-ml). Use slack #applied-ml for quick questions and attach raw response snippets when creating JIRA tickets.
